notes: Line forms: {n} Feyre's narration, first person past tense, shown in italics; {s,e,t} a line spoken aloud (speaker, portrait expression, text); {hint} a game tip on its own card; {choices:[{t,goto,do}]}; {do:[actions]}; {goto}. Any line or choice may carry if_flag, if_not_flag, if_item, if_not_item or if_chapter. Wording is written for the game; the few short book lines kept are listed in quotes.json.

lines.n: It wasn't the dawn that woke me, but a buzzing. A squat female with skin like tree bark was fussing over my breakfast things.

lines.t: Where's Alis?

lines.n: He must have carried me home. All the way home, asleep.

lines.t: What?

lines.n: She turned. I knew the bird mask. But I'd have remembered a faerie who looked like that. I'd have painted her already.

lines.t: Is Alis unwell?
Have you lost your wits? I am Alis.

lines.n: She clucked her tongue, shook her head, and marched off to run my bath.
That couldn't be her. My Alis was fair-skinned and round-cheeked, as High Fae to look at as any of them. Unless... a glamour. Whatever he'd done to my eyes had peeled every glamour away.
But why disguise a whole household? Because I had arrived a terrified human, that was why. Because if I'd seen them as they really were, I'd have barred my door and never stepped outside it again.

do.text: Find Tamlin. He'll be at breakfast in the dining room.

lines.n: The way down was worse. The halls were full of masked faeries I'd never laid eyes on. Some were tall and fair, High Fae like Tamlin. Others were... not. I tried not to stare at those. They seemed the most startled to be noticed.
From my window I'd seen the gardeners, too: insect masks, buzzing wings like oil on water, green-brown skin and limbs far too long.
Lucien, thank the Cauldron, still looked like Lucien.

lines.t: What's wrong?
There are... a great many people. Faeries. Everywhere. When did they all arrive?

lines.n: He bit his lip to keep from smiling.

lines.t: They've been here all along.
But I never heard a thing.
Naturally. We made sure you only saw and heard the ones you had to.
So the night I ran after the puca...
You had an audience.

lines.n: And there I'd been, thinking myself so stealthy. Tiptoeing past faeries who must have laughed themselves sick at the blind human chasing an illusion.

lines.t: It was a valiant effort.
The naga didn't hide from me, though. Or the puca, or the Suriel, or the poor faerie without her wings. Why didn't the glamour cover them?
They aren't of my court, so my glamour couldn't hold them. The puca belongs to the wind and the weather and everything that changes. The naga belong to someone else.
I see.

lines.n: I didn't see at all. Lucien knew it, and chuckled, and I glared at him.

lines.t: You've been noticeably absent again.
Busy. And so, I hear, have you. If I fetch you the moon on a ribbon, is there a kiss in it for me?
Don't be an ass.

lines.n: Lucien was still laughing when he left the room.

lines.t: If I met the Attor again, would I actually see it?
Yes. And it wouldn't be pleasant.
You said it didn't see me in the garden. It's certainly not one of yours. So why not?
Because I threw a glamour over you as we walked in. It couldn't see you, or hear you, or smell you.

lines.n: He looked past me to the window and dragged a hand through his hair.

lines.t: I've done all I can to keep you hidden from things like the Attor. And worse. The sickness is stirring again, and more of them are slipping their leashes.
If you see one, even if it looks harmless, if it makes you uneasy, pretend you don't. Don't speak to it. If it hurt you... what came after would be ugly. For it, and for me. You remember the naga.

lines.n: He wasn't doing this to amuse himself; he was keeping me safe. He couldn't stand the thought of me harmed, or of having to make someone pay for it. Had it cost him something, killing the naga?

lines.t: The sickness is growing again?
Only in other lands, so far. You're safe here.
It isn't my safety I'm worried about.
It will be fine.

lines.n: His eyes softened, but his mouth went thin. I didn't offer to help. I knew he'd never let me.
Still, I remembered the painting I'd given him, and the things he'd said of it. And I wished he would have let me close all the same.
I slept badly. In the morning I gathered up my paints and easel, meaning to give the whole day to the irises round the heron fountain.

do.text: Take your paints out to the irises by the heron fountain.

lines.n: A bright, still morning. Past the reflecting pool, the irises round the heron fountain would be at their best.
My tins and brushes clattered onto the gravel.
A head. A male, High Fae, spiked on the stone heron's upraised bill. The statue was soaked with so much blood it must have been fresh when they drove it on.
Brown eyes bulging. Teeth broken and bloody. The mouth still open on a scream. No mask, so not of the Spring Court. Beyond that, I couldn't tell anything.
I stepped back, and walked straight into something warm and solid.

lines.t: It's me.

lines.n: Lucien stood beside him, pale and grim.

lines.t: Not Autumn Court. I don't know him at all.
Nor do I.

lines.n: His hands closed on my shoulders. A soft, vicious growl ran under his words, but no claws touched me. Lucien waded into the red water of the basin and peered up at that face.

lines.t: They branded him behind the ear. A mountain, with three stars.
The Night Court.

lines.n: The northernmost part of Prythian, if I remembered the mural's map. A land of darkness and starlight.

lines.t: Why would they do this?
The Night Court does as it pleases. They live by their own codes. Their own rotten morals.
Sadistic killers, every one of them. They delight in every kind of torture, and they'd find a stunt like this hilarious.
Hilarious. But not a message?
It's a message, all right. Slipping past our wards and out again, and the blood still wet... That has the Night Court's High Lord written all over it. His idea of fun. The bastard.

lines.n: There was a thick, wet sound of flesh and bone scraping stone as he pulled it free. I'd skinned more animals than I could count. This was nothing like that. Tamlin's other hand settled on my shoulder.
Sixty, seventy feet from the house. That was how close they'd come.

lines.t: You're still safe here. It was only their idea of a prank.
It has nothing to do with the sickness?
Only in that they know it's waking again, and want us to know they're circling like vultures, in case our wards fall any further. I won't let that happen.

lines.n: The masks made it plain enough that nothing could be done against the sickness. I didn't have the heart to say so.

lines.t: They'll get what's coming to them soon enough. With any luck, the sickness will wreck them too.

lines.n: Tamlin growled at him to see to the head, and the gravel crunched as he went.
I crouched for my paints, hands shaking. Tamlin knelt beside me and closed his hands around mine.

lines.t: You're still safe.

lines.n: The Suriel's words came back to me. Stay with the High Lord, and you will be safe. I nodded.

lines.t: It's a show. The Night Court is dangerous, but this was nothing more than its lord amusing himself. Striking at anyone here, at you, would cost him more than he'd gain. And if the sickness tears down the borders and his kind come through with it, we'll be waiting.

choices.t: "Their jokes must have been worse, when we were your slaves."
Say nothing, and gather your brushes.

lines.t: Their jokes must have been even worse when my people were your slaves.

lines.n: A shadow moved behind his eyes.

lines.t: There are days I'm grateful I was only a boy when my father shipped his slaves back over the wall. What little I saw was enough.
Do you remember if they were glad to go?

Yes. They'd never been free, never seen the seasons turn the way you have. Out in the mortal world they hardly knew what to do with themselves. But nearly all of them went gladly. I was glad, too, to watch them leave. My father wasn't.

lines.n: His claws had slid out above his knuckles, though he hadn't moved at all. No wonder he hadn't known what to do with me, when I first came.

lines.t: You're not your father, Tamlin. Or your brothers. You never once made me feel like a prisoner. Or like a piece of property.

lines.n: He nodded, grateful, and the shadows in his face told me there was more to it. About his family, about who he'd been before they died and the title was pushed onto him. I wouldn't pry. Not with so much already weighing on him. He would tell me when he wanted to. He'd given me room and patience; I owed him the same.
I said nothing. I picked up my brushes one by one, and he helped, and neither of us looked at the fountain again.
I couldn't bring myself to paint that day.

Within hours he was called away to one of the borders. Where, and why, he wouldn't say. I could read enough in what he didn't say: the sickness was crawling out of the other courts, straight toward ours.
He stayed away all night, the first night he ever had, and sent Lucien to tell me he was alive. Lucien leaned on that last word so hard that I hardly slept.
I knew where this path ended. My mortal heart, in pieces. And still I couldn't stop. I hadn't been able to since the day of the naga.
Yet I woke the next morning to merry fiddling. The garden was hung with ribbons and streamers, and out on the hills they were building bonfires and raising maypoles.

lines.t: Midsummer. All the courts used to gather for it in the Summer Court, but that's done with, so we hold our own. And you're coming.

lines.n: Alis's people, I'd learned, were called the urisk.

Summer. In all those weeks of painting and dining and wandering the estate at his side, summer had come. At home there'd be a little gathering in the square: shared food, donated ale, a line dance or two. This would be something else entirely.

Tamlin was gone nearly all day. It was late afternoon before I heard his voice, and Lucien's braying laugh, echoing down the halls. I ran to find them, and Alis caught me on the stairs and hauled me back up.

Off came my paint-spattered clothes, and on went a drift of cornflower-blue chiffon, with my hair left loose and a crown of pink and white and blue wildflowers on top. It could have made me feel like a little girl. But months of good food had filled in the sharp angles of me, and the body in the mirror was a woman's. I'd never expected to be anything but sinew and bone.

lines.t: Cauldron boil me. She looks positively Fae.

lines.n: I was too busy checking Tamlin over for blood, for wounds, for any mark the sickness might have left, to thank him. But Tamlin was clean, almost glowing, and unarmed. And smiling at me.

lines.t: You look lovely.
I'm surprised I'm even allowed out tonight.
Unluckily for you and your neck, tonight is only a party.
Do you lie awake at night thinking up tomorrow's clever remarks?
He's right, though. Midsummer is a time of truce, when everyone lets their hair down and simply gets to be a faerie. Not High Fae, not lesser. Just us.
Which means singing, dancing, shocking amounts of drinking. And dallying.

do.text: Midsummer on the lawn. Find something to eat, then follow the music.
